questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The basic principle used behind the working of electron microscope is:
options: Magnifying power of very thin aperture convex lenses.
Electrostatic field created by a beam of electrons.
Using charged mirrors to achieve the desired magnification.
questions.solution:
The working of an electron microscope is based on the wave nature of electrons. According to de Broglie's hypothesis, moving electrons behave as waves. The wavelength of these electron waves is much smaller than that of visible light, which allows for a much higher resolving power and magnification compared to optical microscopes.

Answer: Wave nature of electrons.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The variation of the stopping potential ($V_0$) with the frequency of incident radiation(n) is as given below.
[$n_0$ - threshold frequency. h- Planck's constant e- electronic charge] then the slope of the graph AB with the frequency axis is:
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons is given by:

$K_{\text{max}} = hn - \Phi$

where $h$ is Planck's constant, $n$ is the frequency of incident radiation, and $\Phi$ is the work function of the metal.

We know that $K_{\text{max}} = eV_0$, where $e$ is the charge of an electron and $V_0$ is the stopping potential. Substituting this into the equation, we get:

$eV_0 = hn - \Phi$

$V_0 = \left(\dfrac{h}{e}\right)n - \dfrac{\Phi}{e}$

Comparing this equation with the standard equation of a straight line $y = mx + c$, we have:

$y = V_0$
$x = n$
Slope, $m = \dfrac{h}{e}$

Therefore, the slope of the graph of stopping potential ($V_0$) versus frequency ($n$) is $\dfrac{h}{e}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{h}{e}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When metal of work function 1.4eV is exposed to a radiation, the maximum kinetic energy of the electron emitted is 0.4eV. The stopping potential required is:
questions.solution:
Given maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron, $K_{\max} = 0.4$ eV.

The relation between maximum kinetic energy and stopping potential $V_0$ is given by $K_{\max} = e V_0$.

Substituting the value of $K_{\max}$, we get $e V_0 = 0.4$ eV.

$V_0 = 0.4$ V.

Answer: $0.4$ V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A monochromatic beam of photons of intensity to 1.5 $Wm^{-2}$ and energy 11.2 eV is incident on a material of work function 4.8 eV. What is the maximum speed of photoelectrons emitted due to photoelectric effect if, only 0.53% of the incident photons eject photoelectrons. Given mass of electron $m = 9 \times 10^{-31}$ kg.
questions.solution:
Using Einstein's photoelectric equation:

$K_{\max} = E - \Phi$

Substituting the given values for the energy of the incident photon and the work function:

$K_{\max} = 11.2 \text{ eV} - 4.8 \text{ eV} = 6.4 \text{ eV}$

Converting the maximum kinetic energy into Joules:

$K_{\max} = 6.4 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J} = 10.24 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$

The maximum kinetic energy is related to the maximum speed by $K_{\max} = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_{\max}^2$.

$v_{\max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 K_{\max}}{m}}$

Substituting the mass of the electron $m = 9 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$:

$v_{\max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 10.24 \times 10^{-19}}{9 \times 10^{-31}}}$

$v_{\max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{20.48 \times 10^{12}}{9}}$

$v_{\max} = \dfrac{4.525}{3} \times 10^6 \approx 1.5 \times 10^6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $1.5 \times 10^6\ ms^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the ratio of de Broglie wavelength of an electron to that of proton if the velocity of proton is $\dfrac{1}{6}$ the velocity of electron?
questions.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength is given by $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$.

For an electron, $\lambda_e = \dfrac{h}{m_e v_e}$.

For a proton, $\lambda_p = \dfrac{h}{m_p v_p}$.

The ratio of their wavelengths is:

$\dfrac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} = \dfrac{m_p v_p}{m_e v_e}$

Given that the velocity of the proton is $\dfrac{1}{6}$ the velocity of the electron, we have $v_p = \dfrac{v_e}{6}$, which gives $\dfrac{v_p}{v_e} = \dfrac{1}{6}$.

The mass of a proton is approximately $1836$ times the mass of an electron, so $\dfrac{m_p}{m_e} = 1836$.

Substituting these values into the ratio:

$\dfrac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} = 1836 \times \dfrac{1}{6} = 306$

The ratio of the de Broglie wavelength of the electron to that of the proton is $306:1$.

Answer: $306:1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A plot of kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons from a metal versus the frequency of incident radiation gives a straight line, the intercept of which
A. Depends on the nature of the metal used
B. Depends on the intensity of radiation
C. Depends both on the intensity and the nature of metal used
D. Is a constant and is same for all metals which is independent of the intensity of Incident radiation
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the kinetic energy $K_{max}$ of emitted photoelectrons is given by $K_{max} = h u - \Phi$, where $h$ is Planck's constant, $ u$ is the frequency of incident radiation, and $\Phi$ is the work function of the metal.

Comparing this equation with the equation of a straight line $y = mx + c$, where $y = K_{max}$, $x = u$, $m = h$, and $c = -\Phi$, we see that the intercept on the y-axis is $-\Phi$.

The work function $\Phi$ is a characteristic property of the metal and depends on the nature of the metal used. It is independent of the intensity of the incident radiation.

Answer: A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The de-Broglie wavelength of a neutron having kinetic energy 0.025 eV is $\lambda$. If the kinetic energy of the neutron is reduced to $\dfrac{0.025 \mathrm{eV}}{8}$, its de-Broglie wavelength will be:
questions.solution:
The de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ of a particle with mass $m$ and kinetic energy $K$ is given by the relation $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$.

For the initial state, the wavelength is $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m(0.025 \text{ eV})}}$.

When the kinetic energy is reduced to $K' = \dfrac{0.025 \text{ eV}}{8}$, the new wavelength $\lambda'$ is given by $\lambda' = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m \times \dfrac{0.025 \text{ eV}}{8}}}$.

Simplifying the expression for $\lambda'$:

$\lambda' = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{\dfrac{2m(0.025 \text{ eV})}{8}}} = \sqrt{8} \times \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m(0.025 \text{ eV})}}$.

Since $\sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$, we have $\lambda' = 2\sqrt{2} \lambda$.

Answer: $2 \sqrt{2} \lambda$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following statement is wrong regarding the photo electric effect.
options: The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons emitted depends on the intensity of the incident radiation
Photo electric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident radiation
The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons emitted depends on the frequency of the incident radiation
The value of the stopping potential increases with the increase in frequency of the incident radiation.
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons is given by $K_{max} = h u - \Phi$, where $h$ is Planck's constant, $ u$ is the frequency of incident radiation, and $\Phi$ is the work function of the metal.

From this equation, it is evident that $K_{max}$ depends only on the frequency of the incident radiation $ u$ and the work function $\Phi$ of the material. It does not depend on the intensity of the incident radiation.

The photoelectric current is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident radiation, provided the frequency is above the threshold frequency. This is a correct statement.

The stopping potential $V_s$ is related to the maximum kinetic energy by $eV_s = K_{max} = h u - \Phi$. As the frequency $ u$ increases, $K_{max}$ increases, and consequently, the stopping potential $V_s$ increases. This is a correct statement.

Since the maximum kinetic energy is independent of intensity, the statement that it depends on the intensity of the incident radiation is incorrect.

Answer: The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons emitted depends on the intensity of the incident radiation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the maximum wave length of EM radiation required to move an electron from the valance band to conduction band of a semiconductor? [Given :Energy gap $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{g}}=1.98 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}$; Planck's constant $h=6.6 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{Js}$ ]
questions.solution:
The energy required to move an electron from the valence band to the conduction band is given by the energy gap $E_{g}$. The relationship between the energy of a photon and its wavelength $\lambda$ is given by $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.

To find the maximum wavelength $\lambda_{max}$ required, we use the minimum energy $E_{g}$:

$\lambda_{max} = \dfrac{hc}{E_{g}}$

Given values are $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \text{ Js}$, $E_{g} = 1.98 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$, and the speed of light $c = 3 \times 10^{8} \text{ m/s}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$\lambda_{max} = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{1.98 \times 10^{-19}}$

$\lambda_{max} = \dfrac{19.8 \times 10^{-26}}{1.98 \times 10^{-19}}$

$\lambda_{max} = 10 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} = 10^{-6} \text{ m}$

Answer: $10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: De Broglie wavelength associated with an electron accelerated through a potential difference ' V ' is ' $\lambda$ '. If the accelerating potential is halved, what will be the new wavelength associated with the charged particle?
questions.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ of an electron accelerated through a potential difference $V$ is given by the formula $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}$, where $h$ is Planck's constant, $m$ is the mass of the electron, and $e$ is the charge of the electron.

From this expression, it is evident that $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$.

Let the initial wavelength be $\lambda_1 = \lambda$ at potential $V_1 = V$.

Let the new wavelength be $\lambda_2$ at potential $V_2 = \dfrac{V}{2}$.

Taking the ratio of the two wavelengths:

$\dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{V}{V/2}} = \sqrt{2}$.

Therefore, $\lambda_2 = \sqrt{2} \lambda_1 = \sqrt{2} \lambda$.

Answer: $\sqrt{2} \lambda$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A plot of kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons from a metal versus the frequency of incident radiation gives a straight line, the intercept of which
A. Depends on the nature of the metal used
B. Depends on the intensity of radiation
C. Depends both on the intensity and the nature of metal used
D. Is a constant and is same for all metals which is independent of the intensity of Incident radiation
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the kinetic energy $K_{max}$ of emitted photoelectrons is given by $K_{max} = h u - \Phi$, where $h$ is Planck's constant, $ u$ is the frequency of incident radiation, and $\Phi$ is the work function of the metal.

The equation $K_{max} = h u - \Phi$ represents a straight line of the form $y = mx + c$, where $y = K_{max}$, $x = u$, $m = h$ (slope), and $c = -\Phi$ (intercept).

The intercept on the $y$-axis is $-\Phi$, which is the negative of the work function of the metal. Since the work function $\Phi$ is a characteristic property of the metal, the intercept depends solely on the nature of the metal used.

The intercept is independent of the intensity of the incident radiation, as intensity only affects the number of photoelectrons emitted, not their maximum kinetic energy.

Answer: A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The stopping potential when a metal surface is illuminated by light of wavelength $\lambda$ is 15 V . The stopping potential when the same surface is illuminated by light of wavelength $4 \lambda$ is 3 V . The ratio of threshold wavelength to the initial incident wavelength $\lambda$ is:
questions.solution:
From Einstein's photoelectric equation, the stopping potential $V_s$ is given by $eV_s = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \Phi$, where $\Phi$ is the work function of the metal and $\lambda_0$ is the threshold wavelength such that $\Phi = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}$.

For the first case, $eV_1 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 15e$. Thus, $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 15e$ (Equation 1).

For the second case, $eV_2 = \dfrac{hc}{4\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 3e$. Thus, $\dfrac{hc}{4\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 3e$ (Equation 2).

Subtracting Equation 2 from Equation 1:

$\left( \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{4\lambda} \right) = 15e - 3e = 12e$

$\dfrac{3hc}{4\lambda} = 12e \Rightarrow \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 16e$.

Substituting $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 16e$ into Equation 1:

$16e - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 15e \Rightarrow \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = e$.

Since $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 16e$ and $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = e$, we have $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 16 \left( \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} \right)$, which implies $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{16}{\lambda_0}$.

Therefore, $\dfrac{\lambda_0}{\lambda} = 16$, or the ratio of threshold wavelength to the initial wavelength is $16:1$.

Answer: $16: 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $M$ at rest decays into masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ with non-zero velocities. The ratio of de Broglie wavelengths $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ of the particles is
questions.solution:
The particle of mass $M$ is initially at rest, so its initial momentum is zero. By the law of conservation of linear momentum, the final momenta of the two particles $m_1$ and $m_2$ must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

Let $p_1$ be the magnitude of the momentum of particle $m_1$ and $p_2$ be the magnitude of the momentum of particle $m_2$. Then $p_1 = p_2 = p$.

The de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ of a particle is given by the relation $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$, where $h$ is Planck's constant.

For the two particles, we have $\lambda_1 = \dfrac{h}{p_1}$ and $\lambda_2 = \dfrac{h}{p_2}$.

Since $p_1 = p_2$, it follows that $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$.

Therefore, the ratio $\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = 1$.

Answer: 1:1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Emission of electrons from a metal plate illuminated with monochromatic electromagnetic radiation will always take place provided
options: The work function of the plate is less than the energy of a single photon and the plate is uncharged
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron is given by $K_{max} = h u - \Phi$, where $h u$ is the energy of the incident photon and $\Phi$ is the work function of the metal.

For emission to occur, the energy of the incident photon must be greater than the work function of the metal, i.e., $h u \gt \Phi$. If $h u \lt \Phi$, no electrons are emitted regardless of the intensity of the radiation, because intensity only affects the number of photons incident per unit time, not the energy of individual photons.

If the plate is uncharged, the condition $h u \gt \Phi$ is sufficient for emission. If the plate is negatively charged, the potential barrier for electron emission increases, making it harder for electrons to escape. If the plate is positively charged, it may assist emission, but the fundamental requirement for the photoelectric effect remains that the incident photon energy must exceed the work function of the material.

Answer: The work function of the plate is less than the energy of a single photon and the plate is uncharged

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a beam of 10.6 eV photons of intensity $2.0 \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{m}^2$ falls on a platinum surface of area $1.0 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2$ and work function 5.6 eV . $0.53 \%$ of the incident photons eject photoelectrons. The number of photoelectrons emitted per second is
questions.solution:
Energy of incident photons,
$\begin{aligned} \\ E_1 & =10.6 \mathrm{eV}=10.6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} \\ \\ & =16.96 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} \\ \end{aligned}$
Energy incident per unit area per unit time (intensity) $=2 \mathrm{~J}$
$\therefore$ Number of photons incident on unit area in unit time
$\begin{aligned} \\ & =\frac{2}{16.96 \times 10^{-19}} \\ \\ & =1.18 \times 10^{18} \\ \end{aligned}$
Therefore, number of photons incident per unit time on given area.
$\begin{aligned} \\ \left(1.0 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2\right) & \\ \\ & =\left(1.18 \times 10^{18}\right)\left(1.0 \times 10^{-4}\right) \\ \\ & =1.18 \times 10^{14} \\ \end{aligned}$
But only $0.53 \%$ of incident, photons emit photoelectrons.
$\therefore$ Number of photoelectrons emitted per second,
$\begin{aligned} \\ & n=\left(\frac{0.53}{100}\right)\left(1.18 \times 10^{14}\right) \\ \\ & n=6.25 \times 10^{11} \\ \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The velocity of an electron so that its momentum is equal to that of a photon of wavelength $660 \mathrm{~nm}$ is
questions.solution:
The momentum of a photon is given by $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$.

Given $\lambda = 660 \text{ nm} = 660 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$.

The momentum of an electron is $p = mv$. Equating the two:

$mv = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$

$v = \dfrac{h}{m \lambda}$

Substituting the values $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$, $m = 9.1 imes 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$, and $\lambda = 660 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$:

$v = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{(9.1 \times 10^{-31}) \times (660 \times 10^{-9})}$

$v = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{6006 \times 10^{-40}}$

$v = \dfrac{6.626}{6006} \times 10^{6} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

$v \approx 0.001103 \times 10^{6} \text{ m s}^{-1} = 1103 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Using $h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ for approximation:

$v = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 660 \times 10^{-9}} = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{-34}}{6006 \times 10^{-40}} = \dfrac{6.6}{6006} \times 10^{6} \approx 1098.9 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

This value is approximately $1098 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $1098 \mathrm{~ms} ^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $\mathrm{K}_1$ and $\mathrm{K}_2$ are maximum kinetic energies of photoelectrons emitted when lights of wavelength $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ respectively are incident on a metallic surface. If $\lambda_1=3 \lambda_2$, then
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy $K$ of emitted photoelectrons is given by $K = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \Phi$, where $\Phi$ is the work function of the metal.

For wavelengths $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, we have:
$K_1 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_1} - \Phi$
$K_2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \Phi$

Given $\lambda_1 = 3\lambda_2$, substituting this into the expression for $K_1$:
$K_1 = \dfrac{hc}{3\lambda_2} - \Phi$

We can express $K_2$ as $K_2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \Phi$. Multiplying by $\dfrac{1}{3}$ gives:
$\dfrac{1}{3} K_2 = \dfrac{hc}{3\lambda_2} - \dfrac{\Phi}{3}$

Comparing $K_1$ and $\dfrac{1}{3} K_2$:
$K_1 - \dfrac{1}{3} K_2 = \left( \dfrac{hc}{3\lambda_2} - \Phi \right) - \left( \dfrac{hc}{3\lambda_2} - \dfrac{\Phi}{3} \right)$
$K_1 - \dfrac{1}{3} K_2 = -\Phi + \dfrac{\Phi}{3} = -\dfrac{2\Phi}{3}$

Since the work function $\Phi \gt 0$, it follows that $K_1 - \dfrac{1}{3} K_2 \lt 0$, which implies $K_1 \lt \dfrac{1}{3} K_2$.

Answer: $\mathrm{K}_1\lt \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \mathrm{K}_2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $2 \mathrm{mg}$ has the same wavelength as a neutron moving with a velocity of $3 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. The velocity of the particle is (mass of neutron is $1.67 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{Kg}$)
questions.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ is given by the relation $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$.

Since the particle and the neutron have the same wavelength, we have $\lambda_{p} = \lambda_{n}$, which implies $m_{p} v_{p} = m_{n} v_{n}$.

Given values are:
Mass of particle $m_{p} = 2 \text{ mg} = 2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg}$.
Mass of neutron $m_{n} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$.
Velocity of neutron $v_{n} = 3 \times 10^5 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Substituting these values into the equation $v_{p} = \dfrac{m_{n} v_{n}}{m_{p}}$:

$v_{p} = \dfrac{(1.67 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}) \times (3 \times 10^5 \text{ ms}^{-1})}{2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg}}$

$v_{p} = \dfrac{5.01 \times 10^{-22}}{2 \times 10^{-6}} \text{ ms}^{-1}$

$v_{p} = 2.505 \times 10^{-16} \text{ ms}^{-1}$

Rounding to the nearest provided option, we get $v_{p} = 2.5 \times 10^{-16} \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Answer: $2.5 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A photon emitted during the de-excitation of electron from a state $\mathrm{n}$ to the second excited state in a hydrogen atom, irradiates a metallic electrode of work function $0.5 \mathrm{~eV}$, in a photocell, with a stopping voltage of $0.47 \mathrm{~V}$. Obtain the value of quantum number of the state '$n$'.
questions.solution:
The energy of a photon emitted during the transition from state $n$ to the second excited state ($n_f = 3$) in a hydrogen atom is given by the Rydberg formula:

$E = 13.6 \left( \dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^2} \right) \text{ eV}$

$E = 13.6 \left( \dfrac{1}{3^2} - \dfrac{1}{n^2} \right) = 13.6 \left( \dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{n^2} \right) \text{ eV}$

According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is $K_{max} = E - \Phi$, where $\Phi$ is the work function. Given $K_{max} = e V_s = 0.47 \text{ eV}$ and $\Phi = 0.5 \text{ eV}$:

$0.47 = E - 0.5$

$E = 0.47 + 0.5 = 0.97 \text{ eV}$

Equating the two expressions for $E$:

$13.6 \left( \dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{n^2} \right) = 0.97$

$\dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{n^2} = \dfrac{0.97}{13.6} \approx 0.07132$

$\dfrac{1}{n^2} = \dfrac{1}{9} - 0.07132 \approx 0.11111 - 0.07132 = 0.03979$

$n^2 = \dfrac{1}{0.03979} \approx 25.13$

$n \approx 5$

Answer: 5

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The mass of a particle $\mathrm{A}$ is double that of the particle $\mathrm{B}$ and the kinetic energy of $\mathrm{B}$ is $\dfrac{1}{8}$th that of A then the ratio of the de- Broglie wavelength of A to that of B is:
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$

Given: $m_A = 2m_B$ and $K_B = \dfrac{1}{8}K_A \Rightarrow K_A = 8K_B$

$\dfrac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_B K_B}{m_A K_A}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_B \cdot K_B}{2m_B \cdot 8K_B}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{16}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$\lambda_A : \lambda_B = 1 : 4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The threshold frequency for a metal surface is '$n_0$'. A photo electric current '$I$' is produced when it is exposed to a light of frequency $\left(\dfrac{11}{6}\right) \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{o}}$ and intensity $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{n}}$. If both the frequency and intensity are halved, the new photoelectric current '$\mathrm{I}^1$' will become:
questions.solution:
The photoelectric effect occurs only when the incident frequency $ u$ is greater than or equal to the threshold frequency $ u_0$.

Initially, the incident frequency is $ u_1 = \dfrac{11}{6} u_0$. Since $ u_1 \gt u_0$, photoelectric emission occurs, and the current is $I$.

When the frequency is halved, the new frequency becomes $ u_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} imes \dfrac{11}{6} u_0 = \dfrac{11}{12} u_0$.

Comparing $ u_2$ with the threshold frequency $ u_0$, we observe that $ u_2 = \dfrac{11}{12} u_0 \lt u_0$.

Since the new incident frequency is less than the threshold frequency, no photoelectric emission can take place, regardless of the intensity of the light.

Therefore, the new photoelectric current $I^1$ is $0$.

Answer: $\mathrm{I^1=0}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a certain metal surface is illuminated with light of frequency $v$, the stopping potential for photoelectric current is $V_0$. When the same surface is illuminated by light of frequency $\frac{v}{2}$, the stopping potential is $\frac{V_0}{4}$. The threshold frequency for photoelectric emission is
questions.solution:
We know that, $e V_0=h v-\phi_0$ where, $\quad V_0=$ stopping potential and $\quad v=$ frequency of light.
Case II $\frac{e V_0}{4}=\frac{h v}{2}-\phi_0$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\begin{array}{rlrl} & h v-\phi_0 =2 h v-4 \phi_0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & h v =3 \phi_0 \Rightarrow h v=3 h v_0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad v_0 & =\frac{h v}{3 h} \Rightarrow v_0=\frac{v}{3} \end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Let $K_1$ be the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons emitted by light of wavelength $\lambda_1$ and $K_2$ corresponding to wavelength $\lambda_2$. If $\lambda_1=2 \lambda_2$, then
questions.solution: Substituting $\lambda_1=2 \lambda_2$ in Eq. (i), we get $\begin{aligned} & K_1=\frac{h c}{2 \lambda_2}-W \\ \Rightarrow \quad & K_1=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{h c}{\lambda_2}\right)-W=\frac{1}{2}\left(K_2+W\right)-W \\ \Rightarrow \quad & K_1=\frac{K_2}{2}-\frac{W}{2} \\ & K_1 \lt \frac{K_2}{2} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle at rest decays in to two particles of mass $m_1$ and $m_2$ and move with velocities $v_1$ and $v_2$. The ratio of their de Broglie wave length $\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$ is:
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the parent particle be $M$. Since the parent particle is at rest, the initial momentum is zero. By the law of conservation of linear momentum, the magnitudes of the momenta of the two decay products must be equal.

$p_1 = p_2 = p$

The de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ of a particle is given by the relation $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$, where $h$ is Planck's constant.

For the two particles, the wavelengths are $\lambda_1 = \dfrac{h}{p_1}$ and $\lambda_2 = \dfrac{h}{p_2}$.

Taking the ratio of the wavelengths:

$\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{h/p_1}{h/p_2} = \dfrac{p_2}{p_1}$

Since $p_1 = p_2$, we have $\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{p}{p} = 1$.

Therefore, the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths is $1 : 1$.

Answer: 1 : 1

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the photoelectric experiment, the frequency of the incident radiation is doubled. What will be its effect on the photoelectric current?
questions.solution:
The photoelectric current in a photoelectric effect experiment depends on the intensity of the incident radiation, which corresponds to the number of photons incident per unit time per unit area. The frequency of the incident radiation determines the energy of each individual photon, given by $E = h\nu$.

Increasing the frequency of the incident radiation increases the kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons, provided the frequency remains above the threshold frequency. However, the number of photoelectrons emitted per second depends only on the number of incident photons per second, not on their individual energy.

Since the intensity of the incident radiation is not changed by doubling the frequency, the number of photons incident per unit time remains constant. Consequently, the number of photoelectrons emitted per unit time remains unchanged, and thus the photoelectric current remains constant.

Answer: Photoelectric current will not change.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When a certain metal surface is illuminated with light of frequency $\nu$, the stopping potential for photoelectric current is $V_0$. When the same surface is illuminated by light of frequency $\dfrac{\nu}{2}$, the stopping potential is $\dfrac{V_0}{4}$. The threshold frequency for photoelectric emission is
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy $K_{max}$ is given by $K_{max} = h u - \phi$, where $\phi = h u_0$ is the work function and $ u_0$ is the threshold frequency.

The stopping potential $V_0$ is related to the maximum kinetic energy by $eV_0 = K_{max}$. Thus, $eV_0 = h u - h u_0$.

For the first case, $eV_0 = h u - h u_0$. (Equation 1)

For the second case, with frequency $\dfrac{ u}{2}$ and stopping potential $\dfrac{V_0}{4}$, we have $e\left(\dfrac{V_0}{4} ight) = h\left(\dfrac{ u}{2} ight) - h u_0$. (Equation 2)

Multiplying Equation 2 by 4, we get $eV_0 = 2h u - 4h u_0$. (Equation 3)

Equating Equation 1 and Equation 3, we have $h u - h u_0 = 2h u - 4h u_0$.

Rearranging the terms, $3h u_0 = h u$, which simplifies to $ u_0 = \dfrac{ u}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{ u}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Let $K_1$ be the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons emitted by light of wavelength $\lambda_1$ and $K_2$ corresponding to wavelength $\lambda_2$. If $\lambda_1=2 \lambda_2$, then
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy $K$ of emitted photoelectrons is given by $K = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi$, where $\phi$ is the work function of the metal.

For wavelength $\lambda_1$, $K_1 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_1} - \phi$.

For wavelength $\lambda_2$, $K_2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \phi$.

Given $\lambda_1 = 2\lambda_2$, we substitute $\lambda_1$ in the expression for $K_1$:

$K_1 = \dfrac{hc}{2\lambda_2} - \phi$.

Since $\phi \gt 0$, we have $\dfrac{hc}{2\lambda_2} - \phi \lt \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} \right)$.

Also, $K_2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \phi$, which implies $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} = K_2 + \phi$.

Substituting this into the expression for $K_1$:

$K_1 = \dfrac{K_2 + \phi}{2} - \phi = \dfrac{K_2}{2} - \dfrac{\phi}{2}$.

Since $\phi \gt 0$, it follows that $K_1 \lt \dfrac{K_2}{2}$.

Answer: $K_1 \lt K_2 / 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Ultraviolet light of wavelength $99 \text{ nm}$ falls on a metal plate of work function $1.0 \text{ eV}$. If the mass of the electron is $9.1 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$, the de Broglie wavelength of the fastest photoelectron emitted is
questions.solution:
$E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1242\,\text{eV·nm}}{99\,\text{nm}} \approx 12.54\,\text{eV}$

$K_{max} = E - \Phi = 12.54 - 1.0 = 11.54\,\text{eV}$

Using the de Broglie wavelength formula for electrons:

$\lambda_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{150}{K_{max}(\text{in eV})}}\,\text{\AA} = \sqrt{\dfrac{150}{11.54}}\,\text{\AA} = \sqrt{13.0}\,\text{\AA} \approx 3.6\,\text{\AA} = 0.36\,\text{nm}$

Correct option: (4)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If $K_1$ and $K_2$ are maximum kinetic energies of photoelectrons emitted when lights of wavelengths $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, respectively incident on a metallic surface and $\lambda_1=3 \lambda_2$, then
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy $K$ of emitted photoelectrons is given by $K = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi$, where $\phi$ is the work function of the metal.

For the first wavelength $\lambda_1$, $K_1 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_1} - \phi$.

For the second wavelength $\lambda_2$, $K_2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \phi$.

Given $\lambda_1 = 3\lambda_2$, we substitute this into the expression for $K_1$:

$K_1 = \dfrac{hc}{3\lambda_2} - \phi = \dfrac{1}{3} \left( \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - 3\phi \right)$.

Since $K_2 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} - \phi$, we have $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_2} = K_2 + \phi$.

Substituting this into the expression for $K_1$:

$K_1 = \dfrac{1}{3} (K_2 + \phi - 3\phi) = \dfrac{K_2 - 2\phi}{3} = \dfrac{K_2}{3} - \dfrac{2\phi}{3}$.

Since $\phi \gt 0$, it follows that $K_1 \lt \dfrac{K_2}{3}$.

Answer: $K_1 \lt \left(\dfrac{K_2}{3}\right)$

questions.q: The momentum of the proton is one-fourth the momentum of the electron. What is the ratio of the de-Broglie wavelength of an electron to that of a proton?
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} \Rightarrow \dfrac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} = \dfrac{p_p}{p_e}$

Given $p_p = \dfrac{1}{4}p_e \Rightarrow \dfrac{p_p}{p_e} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

$\dfrac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Correct option: (4)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: From the figure describing photoelectric effect, we may infer correctly that
options: $\mathrm{Na}$ and $\mathrm{Al}$ both have the same threshold frequency
Maximum kinetic energy for both the metals depends linearly on the frequency
the stopping potential are different for $\mathrm{Na}$ and $\mathrm{Al}$ for the same change in frequency
questions.solution:
From Einstein's photoelectric equation: $eV_s = h u - \Phi \Rightarrow V_s = \dfrac{h}{e} u - \dfrac{\Phi}{e}$

This is a linear equation in $ u$ with slope $\dfrac{h}{e}$, which is universal (same for all metals).

(1) Na and Al have different x-intercepts ⇒ different threshold frequencies. So (1) is incorrect.

(2) $K_{max} = h u - \Phi$, which is linear in $ u$ for any metal. So (2) is correct.

(3) Slope is the same for both ⇒ same change in $V_s$ for same change in $ u$. So (3) is incorrect.

(4) Na has a lower threshold frequency ⇒ Na is more photosensitive than Al. So (4) is incorrect.

Correct option: (2)

questions.solution:
When a charged particle of charge $q$ is accelerated through a potential $V$, then de-Broglie wavelength is given as
$\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m q V}}\Rightarrow \quad \lambda \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{m q}}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\lambda_{\alpha}}{\lambda_{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{p}}{m_{\alpha}}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{q_{p}}{q_{\alpha}}}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\lambda_{\alpha}}{\lambda}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{p}}{4 m_{p}}} \sqrt{\frac{q_{p}}{2 q_{p}}} \quad\left[\begin{array}{c}\because m_{\alpha}=4 m_{p} \\ \text { and } q_{\alpha}=2 q_{p}\end{array}\right]\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\lambda_{\alpha}}{\lambda}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\Rightarrow \quad \lambda_{\alpha}=\frac{\lambda}{2 \sqrt{2}}$

When same surface is illuminated by light of wavelength $2 \lambda$, then stopping potential becomes $V_{s}$. The value of threshold wavelength for photoelectric emission will be
questions.solution:
According to first situation wavelength of incident radiation,

\lambda_{1}=\lambda

Stopping potential, $V_{01}=3 V_{\mathrm{s}}$
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation,

\begin{array}{ll} 
& K_{\max }=h v_{1}-\phi \\
\Rightarrow \quad & e V_{01}=\frac{h c}{\lambda_{1}}-\frac{h c}{\lambda_{0}} \\
& {\left[\text { where, } \lambda_{0}=\right.\text { threshold wavelength.] }} \\
\Rightarrow \quad & e \cdot 3 V_{s}=h c\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}}\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad & 3 V_{s} e=h c\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}}\right)
\end{array}

According to second situation, wavelength of incident radiation,

\lambda_{2}=2 \lambda

Stopping potential, $V_{02}=V_{S}$
Again, Einstein's photelectric equation,

\begin{gathered}
K_{\max }=h \mathrm{v}_{2}-\phi \\
\Rightarrow \quad e V_{02}=h c\left(\frac{1}{\lambda_{2}}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}}\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad e V_{s}=h c\left(\frac{1}{2 \lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}}\right)
\end{gathered}

Dividing Eq. (i) by Eq (ii), we get

\begin{aligned}
&3=\frac{\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}}}{\frac{1}{2 \lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}}} \\
&\Rightarrow \quad \\
&\Rightarrow \quad \frac{3}{2 \lambda}-\frac{3}{\lambda_{0}}=\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda_{0}} \\
&\lambda_{0}=4 \lambda
\end{aligned}

questions.q: The energy that should be added to an electron to reduce its de-Broglie wavelength from $1 \mathrm{~nm}$ to $0.5 \mathrm{~nm}$ is
questions.solution:
Given, initial value of de-Broglie wavelength,
$\lambda_{1}=1 \mathrm{~nm}=1 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}$
Final value of de-Broglie wavelength,
$\lambda_{2}=0.5 \mathrm{~nm}=0.5 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}$
de-Broglie wavelength in terms of energy $E$ is given as
$\begin{aligned}
& \lambda &=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m E}} \\
& \therefore & \lambda & \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{E}} \\
\Rightarrow & & \frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}} &=\sqrt{\frac{E_{2}}{E_{1}}}
\end{aligned}$
where, $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ are initial and final energy,
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1 \times 10^{-9}}{0.5 \times 10^{-9}}=\sqrt{\frac{E_{2}}{E_{1}}}\Rightarrow \quad 2=\sqrt{\frac{E_{2}}{E_{1}}}\Rightarrow \quad E_{2}=4 E_{1}\therefore$ Addition of energy $=E_{2}-E_{1}=4 E_{1}-E_{1}=3 E_{1}\quad=$ thrice the initial energy

questions.q: A proton and an alpha particle are subjected to same potential difference $V$. Their de-Broglie wavelengths $\lambda_{p}, \lambda_{\alpha}$ will be in the ratio
questions.solution:
T
he de-Broglie wavelength of a particle is given by
$\lambda=\frac{h}{m v}=\frac{h}{p}$
The momentum of proton,
$p_{p}=\sqrt{2 m E}=\sqrt{2 m e V}$
Similarly, for $\alpha$ - particle,
$\begin{aligned}
p_{\alpha} &-\sqrt{2 \times 4 m \times 2 e \times V} \\
&=\sqrt{16 m e V} \\
\therefore \quad \frac{\lambda_{p}}{\lambda_{\alpha}} &=\frac{p_{\alpha}}{p_{p}}=\frac{\sqrt{16 m e V}}{\sqrt{2 m e V}}=\sqrt{8} \\
&=2 \sqrt{2}: 1
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A body accelerates from rest with a uniform acceleration $a$ for a time $t$. The uncertainty in $a$ is $8 \%$ and the uncertainty in $t$ is $4 \%$. The uncertainty in the speed is
questions.solution:
Given, uncertainity in acceleration, $\frac{\Delta a}{a} \times 100=8 \%$
Uncertainity in time, $\frac{\Delta t}{t} \times 100=4 \%$
Since, body starts motion from rest, hence by the first equation of motion,

\begin{aligned}
v &=u+a t \\
v &=0+a t \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\Delta v}{v} &=\frac{\Delta a}{a}+\frac{\Delta t}{t} \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\Delta v}{v} \times 100 &=\frac{\Delta a}{a} \times 100+\frac{\Delta t}{t} \times 100 \\
&=8 \%+4 \%=12 \%
\end{aligned}
